study.title: Isaiah 4 - Purification, Restoration and Protection of Zion
study.overview: Isaiah 4 closes the picture of judgment initiated in the previous chapter with a striking turn to hope. After the extreme humiliation described in the first verses, the text announces a purified remnant, separated to God and protected by his presence. The central image is not only the survival of some, but the renewal of the relationship between the LORD and his people: cleansing of guilt, holiness for those who remain, and a divine covering that recalls the exodus. The chapter presents this restoration as comfort for those who escape judgment and as a sign that the glory of God will again dwell among them.

outline.title: Extreme scarcity and social shame
outline.explanation: The first verse continues the description of devastation begun before: there will be so few men that several women will seek a single husband. The scene shows the breaking of the social order and the desperate urgency for protection and honor, albeit in humiliating conditions.

outline.title: The remnant will be purified and holy
outline.explanation: From verse 2, the tone changes to promise. The "New of the Lord" and the "fruit of the earth" point to a new beginning for those who escape. These survivors will be called saints, because the LORD will wash the uncleanness of Zion and remove the blame of Jerusalem through an action of judgment and purification.

outline.title: God's protective presence on Zion
outline.explanation: The last two verses describe the restoration in language of divine presence. A cloud of day, smoke and fire at night remind you of God's continued protection in the exodus. This presence becomes a tent of shadow, refuge and shelter against the dangers of heat, storm and rain.

study.context: The notes link this chapter to the scenario of national crisis and war already exposed in the previous chapter. Tyndale and Adam Clarke observe that the devastation would leave Jerusalem with very few men, making the scene of verse 1 a consequence of war and calamity. At the same time, the same notes understand that Isaiah 4:2-6 announces a hope linked to the remnant and the restoration of Zion, with echoes of the exodus from Egypt. Matthew Henry also reads the chapter as a transition from the threat to the promise, seeing in it a consolation amidst the judgment and an anticipation of the work of the Messiah, without denying that the text may have close historical reference to the crises of Judah.
study.theology: Theologically, the chapter unites judgment and grace. Judgment exposes human shame, loss of security and the need for purification; grace preserves a remnant and makes it holy. The text insists that restoration is not born of the capacity of the people, but from the action of the LORD: he washes, cleans, creates protection and dwells with his people. The expression "Renew" was understood by some commentators as the renewed remnant itself, and by others as a reference to the Messiah; in both cases, the main idea is the divine origin of the new life. The final image of the cloud and fire shows that God's presence is not only symbolic: it guards, guides and covers the people with real care. Holiness, therefore, is not mere religious label, but a condition of belonging to restored Zion, where names are among those who live.

scholarViews.insight: The "New of the LORD." in Isaiah 4:2 is presented as the beginning of a new stage for the remnant after exile; the images of cloud and fire in 4:5-6 resume the exodus and indicate God's continued protection and presence.
Matthew Henry sees Isaiah 4:2-6 as a promise of restoration of Jerusalem's peace, purity, justice, and security in the days of the Messiah, in contrast to the judgment of verse 1.
Adam Clarke understands Isaiah 4:6 as a figure of a tent that offers shadow, refuge and shelter, that is, a concrete image of divine protection from heat, storm and rain.

questions: What does the contrast between public shame and the rest's holiness teach about how God treats sin and restoration?
How do images of cloud, fire and tent help to understand God's protective presence in the midst of the crisis?
How does the idea of being written to life confronts an external faith only and calls to perseverance?
study.practice: This chapter invites the reader to abandon any confidence in human appearance, number or security, and to seek the purification that comes from the Lord. In practice, this means recognizing one's impurity, valuing holiness as a mark of belonging to God and relying on his daily presence as a protection. In times of instability, concrete application is to live with repentance, hope and fidelity, remembering that true security is not in the favorable circumstance, but in the presence of God who covers his people.
study.uncertainty: The notes do not solve in a unique way who is exactly the "Renew of the LORD" in Isaiah 4:2: some readings apply it to the restored remnant, and others to the Messiah. Nor is there a sufficient basis in the notes to accurately define the immediate historical reach of each image; therefore, the study treats these possibilities as interpretations, not as absolute conclusions.
